docs.title: Run the checks
docs.text:
Check Command Run it Offline tests pytest before every commit Lint and format ruff check . and ruff format --check . before every commit Recordings replay to the same results python tests/record.py --refresh-expected, then git diff --stat tests/data/recordings must print nothing after a change to plbbg.py Minimum dependencies see below before a pull request that changes plbbg.py Docs build mkdocs build --strict after a change to docs/ or to a public docstring Live tests pytest --bbg when you have a Bloomberg Terminal on this machine

The recordings check repeats what pytest does, but more strictly: pytest compares numbers with a tolerance, and git diff shows every difference.

The offline tests must also pass on the oldest supported versions (Python 3.12, polars 1.7.1, blpapi 3.24.2). Build that environment outside the repository and leave the project environment alone:

MIN=~/venvs/plbbg-min    # any directory outside the repository
uv venv $MIN --python 3.12
uv pip install --python $MIN --no-config \
    --index https://blpapi.bloomberg.com/repository/releases/python/simple/ \
    --index https://pypi.org/simple \
    -e . pytest pytest-cov pyyaml "polars==1.7.1" "blpapi==3.24.2"
$MIN/bin/python -m pytest tests/unit -m no_bbg

On Windows the interpreter of that environment is Scripts\python.exe instead of bin/python.

How the tests are organised, and in which order to read the live tests as a tour of the library, is in tests/README.md.

docs.title: Capture a failing case and turn it into an offline test
docs.text:
The call and the names in this recipe are examples; use those of your case.

  1. Get the raw answer. Run the failing call with debug=True, or ask the user who reported it to do so:

    with BQuery(debug=True) as bq:
    bq.bdp(["IBM US Equity"], ["NAME", "NOT_A_FIELD"])

    Every request writes one JSON file to debug_cases/ in the working directory, for example ReferenceDataRequest_20261116_201008_297370.json, also when the call raises. The file holds the request, every message Bloomberg sent back, and the library versions; Find where a bug is shows one. BQuery(debug="some/dir") writes to that directory.

  2. Make it small and public. The repository is public. Cut the answer down by hand to what shows the problem: at most three securities and five rows where the case allows it. Replace instruments and names that are the user's own by well-known ones, in the request and in the answer alike. Keep the markers that hold dates, such as {"$date": "2024-01-02"}: the replay turns them back into dates. Never commit debug_cases/ itself.

  3. Store it as a recording. Copy the file to tests/data/recordings/<method>/<short_name>.json, and add the call under the same name to SCENARIOS in tests/recordings.py:

    "bdp/unknown_field_next_to_known": lambda bq: bq.bdp(
    ["IBM US Equity"], ["NAME", "NOT_A_FIELD"]
),

    If nobody can record this answer again (the user's own instruments, a market state that is gone), also add the name to CONVERTED in the same file. Then python tests/record.py leaves the file alone.

    From now until step 5, tests/unit/test_recordings.py fails for the new scenario with KeyError: 'expected'. That is correct: the file does not say yet what the call should give.

  4. Write the test that shows the bug, in tests/unit/test_<method>.py:

    def test_bdp_unknown_field_next_to_known_gives_a_null_column():
    bq, _ = replay("bdp/unknown_field_next_to_known")

    df = bq.bdp(["IBM US Equity"], ["NAME", "NOT_A_FIELD"])

    assert df["NOT_A_FIELD"].to_list() == [None]

    replay (in tests/support.py) returns a BQuery whose fake session answers the next request with the recorded messages. Run the test and see it fail.

  5. Fix the code, then store the result the call now gives:

    python tests/record.py --refresh-expected bdp/unknown_field_next_to_known

    This replays the answer, writes the result into the file as "expected", and replaces server names in Bloomberg's error details. Read the file once more, then run pytest: tests/unit/test_recordings.py now replays the new scenario together with all the others.

A recording made this way works like one recorded live. It differs in two harmless ways: it has no "scenario" and "call" keys, and a BQL answer stays one long JSON string instead of readable JSON.

docs.title: Fix a parsing bug
docs.text:
1. Find the parser in the method table and open a recording of that method to see the shape of the payloads.

  2. Reproduce the bug in a test. Replay a recording as in the recipe above, or write the payload by hand when a few lines are enough:

    def test_bdp_security_without_field_data_gives_a_null():
    payload = {"securityData": [{"security": "IBM US Equity", "fieldData": {}}]}
    bq = fake_bq([answer(payload)])

    df = bq.bdp(["IBM US Equity"], ["NAME"])

    assert df["NAME"].to_list() == [None]

    fake_bq and answer are in tests/support.py. The files tests/unit/test_bdp.py to test_bsrch.py show both kinds of test.

  3. Fix the parser and run pytest.

  4. Run python tests/record.py --refresh-expected and read git diff tests/data/recordings. Only the scenarios whose result you meant to change may differ.
  5. If users can notice the fix, add a line to CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Add an option
docs.text:
A Bloomberg request option needs no new code. options={"periodicitySelection": "MONTHLY"} reaches the request through _set_options, under Bloomberg's own element name.

The offline tests build real blpapi requests on a reduced, hand-written schema, tests/data/schemas/refdata_test.xml. An option that the schema does not list raises NotFoundException there. To test a request with a new option, add the <element> to the request type in that file, then assert on the request in tests/unit/test_requests.py with request_sent_by.

A new keyword argument of a public method goes the same way as the existing ones: check it in step 1, set it in step 2, test the request in tests/unit/test_requests.py, describe it in the docstring and in docs/usage/<method>.md, and add it to CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Add a new request type
docs.text:
1. Write the public method on BQuery in the five steps, after the method it resembles most.
  2. Add a numbered section for it below the class with its _parse_<name> function, and add the method to the table and the section list in the module docstring.
  3. Make the request testable offline. For //blp/refdata, add the operation and its request and response types to tests/data/schemas/refdata_test.xml. For another service there is no offline schema; the tests use a MagicMock service, as tests/unit/test_bsrch.py does.
  4. Add scenarios to SCENARIOS in tests/recordings.py and record them at a Terminal: python tests/record.py <name>/. List a scenario in VOLATILE if its data changes from run to run, and in CONTRACT if a live test should watch the format of its answer.
  5. Add tests/unit/test_<name>.py (offline, end to end) and tests/integration/test_integration_<name>.py (live).
  6. Document it: a Google-style docstring with an example (docs/api.md renders it), a page docs/usage/<name>.md listed in mkdocs.yml, a section in README.md, a line in CHANGELOG.md, and a row in the tables of this page.

docs.title: Re-record or refresh recordings
docs.text:
A recording is one file: the request, the raw messages, and "expected", the result the call gave.

  • You changed the output on purpose (no Terminal needed). Run python tests/record.py --refresh-expected; it replays every recording and rewrites only "expected". Add name prefixes to limit it, for example python tests/record.py --refresh-expected bql/. Review git diff tests/data/recordings before you commit.
  • You need a fresh answer from Bloomberg (Terminal needed). Run python tests/record.py bdp/ bql/syntax_error for the scenarios whose names start with these prefixes, or python tests/record.py for all. Scenarios in VOLATILE change on every run; scenarios in CONVERTED are skipped.
  • You suspect Bloomberg changed a format. pytest --bbg includes tests/integration/test_contract.py, which asks Bloomberg again for the scenarios in CONTRACT and compares the shape of the fresh answer with the recording.
  • You changed the dump format in _write_debug_dump. Every recording is a dump, so all of them have to be recorded again. Avoid it.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Users must not be surprised. Method names, parameters, column names, dtypes, exception types and the wording of log messages are part of the interface; tests assert on them. A change that users can notice goes into CHANGELOG.md.
  • One file, plain functions. Being able to open plbbg.py and follow a call from request to DataFrame is the main strength of the library. Prefer a function to a new class, and do not split the file.
  • Comments say why. When a comment explains a Bloomberg quirk, name the recording that shows it.
  • Ruff checks and formats the code (pyproject.toml): line length 89, docstrings required in the package but not in tests, at most six arguments per function.
  • Public methods keep Google-style docstrings with an example and its output.
  • Diagnostics go through logger, never print.
  • No new dependencies, at runtime or for development. Python 3.12+, polars 1.7.1+, blpapi 3.24.2+.
  • Tests check one behavior each, and the name states the scenario and the expected result, for example test_bdh_weekend_range_returns_empty_frame_with_columns. They go through the public methods with the fake session; they do not patch private functions. Offline test modules set pytestmark = pytest.mark.no_bbg, live ones pytest.mark.requires_bbg.
  • Recordings stay small and public: well-known instruments, at most three securities and five rows where the scenario allows it, no machine names.
  • Releases are the maintainer's: do not bump the version, tag or publish.

docs.title: Before you open a pull request
docs.text:
1. pytest, ruff check . and ruff format --check . pass.
  2. python tests/record.py --refresh-expected changes no recording, or only the recordings whose result you meant to change.
  3. If you changed plbbg.py, the offline tests also pass on the minimum dependencies.
  4. A bug fix comes with a test that failed before the fix.
  5. A change that users can notice has a line under "Unreleased" in CHANGELOG.md, and the docstring and the page in docs/usage/ say what the code now does.
  6. The version number is untouched.

AT1 Bond Valuation¶
docs.text:
© 2025 Marek Ozana

This notebook is a small, opinionated workflow for relative value screening in the AT1 universe using polars-bloomberg and interactive Altair charts.

We pull a bond universe (IDs, tickers, ratings, duration, back-end spread, z-spread) and then visualize how z-spread behaves as a function of:

  • Back-end spread (BE) and
  • Duration (Dur)

Both views include a simple fit. Bonds above the trend line are “cheap” on that axis (wider than the model would suggest), and bonds below the line are “rich”.

The two scatter plots are linked: clicking a point in one chart highlights the same bond in the other view, making it easy to spot names that look cheap (or rich) in both dimensions.

docs.title: CET1 vs Requirements and AT1 Trigger levels
CET1 vs Requirements and AT1 Trigger levels¶
docs.text:
© 2025 Marek Ozana

This notebook is a small end-to-end example of using polars-bloomberg to pull regulatory capital metrics from BQL and chart them for a universe of European banks.

We compare three CET1-related levels:

  • CET1 (reported): the bank’s current Common Equity Tier 1 ratio (what it has).
  • CET1 requirement (“review” / SREP): the supervisory CET1 requirement level (what it must meet under review-driven requirements).
  • AT1 trigger: the contractual CET1 trigger level associated with Additional Tier 1 (CoCo) instruments (the “oh no” line where conversion/write-down mechanics may be activated).

Interpretation:

  • The vertical gap CET1 − requirement is “headroom” against supervisory requirements.
  • The gap CET1 − AT1 trigger is distance to the contractual AT1 trigger (not a regulatory buffer).
  • Field definitions vary by jurisdiction and data source. Treat these as indicative and sanity-check against bank disclosures when precision matters.

docs.title: Bank Capital, Asset Quality and Profitability¶
docs.text:
© 2025 Marek Ozana

This notebook pulls quarterly fundamentals for a panel of large European banks and visualizes three core health signals:

  • Capital (CET1 ratio): how much loss-absorbing capital banks have (higher is better)
  • Asset quality (NPL ratio): how much of the loan book is non-performing (lower is better)
  • Profitability (ROE): how efficiently equity is turned into earnings (higher is better)

In the chart below, the line shows the cross-bank average over time and the shaded band shows the dispersion across banks. The big picture is simple: European banks are currently better capitalized, have cleaner loan books (lower NPLs), and are generating higher ROE than in most of the post-crisis period.

docs.title: Credit Spreads vs Equity Cushion
Credit Spreads vs Equity Cushion¶
docs.text:
© 2025 Marek Ozana

This notebook uses polars-bloomberg to study how bond spreads relate to a company’s equity cushion, (EV-NetDebt) / EV

We plot each issuer as a scatter point using average z-spread per year of duration versus equity cushion and highlight the typical “hockey-stick” pattern: spreads are fairly stable at healthy cushions, then widen rapidly when the cushion becomes thin.

Implementation detail: in Bloomberg BQL we map each bond to its issuer fundamentals via fundamentalTicker (mapby=LINEAGE), then group by ticker and rating to aggregate bond-level spread/duration and issuer-level fundamentals into one issuer datapoint.

docs.title: Regional PE Valuation
Regional PE Valuation¶
docs.text:
© 2026 Jim Domeij

This calculates 10-year P/E valuation statistics (average, standard deviation, minimum and maximum) for major equity regions. Current levels are compared to these statistics to assess the relative expansiveness vs history and other regions.

The BQL query builds a shared 10-year date range, defines a reusable forward P/E series, and computes #avg, #std, #min, #max, plus the latest value #last for each index in the universe. BQL returns a Polars DataFrame with ID and those five fields, which are renamed for plotting.

The chart visualizes each region’s distribution using a box for average ±1 standard deviation, whiskers for min/max, a diamond for the average, and a triangle for the latest value.

docs.text:
© 2026 Jim Domeij

Uses the powerful calendar() function to retrieve US economic data releases from the past two month across multiple sectors, excluding low-relevance series and assessing how each release has surprised relative to Bloomberg’s median survey forecast. This provides an overview of recent US economic momentum versus consensus expectations, with the ability to drill down into the details of individual data releases.

docs.title: BDIB – Bloomberg Data Intraday Bar
docs.text: bdib() fetches pre-aggregated intraday bars directly from Bloomberg, so you can work with 1- to 1440-minute candles without managing tick-level aggregation yourself. Each bar is returned as a row of a Polars DataFrame; its time is the start of the bar, as a naive datetime (no time zone) holding UTC.

docs.title: When to use BDIB
docs.text:
• You need intraday OHLCV bars for a single security over a specific time window.
  • You want Bloomberg to enforce consistent interval lengths (e.g., 5-, 15-, 60-minute bars).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• start_datetime and end_datetime can be naive or timezone-aware. Naive values are treated as UTC; aware values are converted to UTC before the request is sent. A date means midnight, and an ISO 8601 string ("2024-01-02T08:00:00") is sent as it is.
  • Supported event_type values: TRADE, BID, ASK, BEST_BID, BEST_ASK.
  • Bloomberg enforces the interval range (1-1440 minutes). A request outside that range raises BloombergError with Bloomberg's unspecific message: Response error: Data not available from service. [nid:…] (NOT_AVAILABLE).
  • An unknown security raises BloombergError too (unlike bdp() and bdh(), which give nulls and a warning). A window without bars, for example one older than the few months of intraday history Bloomberg keeps, gives an empty frame that keeps its columns.
  • Optional overrides and options parameters work the same way as in bdp() and bdh()

docs.title: BQL
docs.text:
Use Case: Run more advanced queries to screen securities, calculate analytics (like moving averages), or pull fundamental data with complex conditions.

Returns: The bql() method returns a BqlResult object, which:

  • Acts like a list of Polars DataFrames (one for each item in BQL get statement).
  • Provides a .combine() method to merge DataFrames. With no arguments it preserves the legacy behavior of joining on common columns. Use .combine(on=...) to join only on explicit keys such as "ID" or ["ID", "DATE"].

A query that BQL rejects, for example for a syntax error, does not raise: bql() returns an empty BqlResult, logs the message and keeps it in result.errors; combine() on it raises ValueError with that message. A screen that matches nothing gives the same empty result; its message ("No results match ...") is logged as a warning, not an error.

docs.text:

with BQuery() as bq:
    results = bq.bql("get(name, px_last) for(['IBM US Equity'])")

n=2

We can use combine() method to join the results into single dataframe: 

>>> combined_df = results.combine(on="ID")
>>> print(combined_df)
Output:

By default, combine() keeps the historical behavior and joins each result DataFrame on all common column names. This is convenient for simple BQL results, but it can be too broad when several item tables share metadata columns such as DATE, CURRENCY, PERIOD, VALUE, or MULTIPLIER.

A row whose shared columns hold nulls matches nothing and appears twice, once from each side: for example a security for which BQL has no DATE.

with BQuery() as bq:
    results = bq.bql(
        "get(px_last, px_volume) for(['IBM US Equity', 'NOT A SECURITY Equity'])"
    )

For safer joins, pass the intended key columns explicitly; combine(on="ID") gives one row per security:

# Join only by security ID. Other common columns are kept as data columns.
combined_df = results.combine(on="ID")

# Join by a compound key when both columns are true row identifiers.
combined_df = results.combine(on=["ID", "DATE"])

# Use Polars join names. "full" is the default for explicit joins.
combined_df = results.combine(on="ID", how="inner")

If non-key columns overlap when using on=..., they are preserved with suffixes based on the BQL item name, for example DATE_#ret_1d. To fail instead of suffixing overlapping non-key columns, use:

combined_df = results.combine(on="ID", allow_common_columns=False)

docs.text:
The following example shows handling of two data-items with different length. The first dataframe describes the segments (and has length 5 in this case), while the second dataframe contains time series. One can join the dataframes on common columns and pivot the segments into columns as shown below: 

# revenue per segment
query = """
    let(#segment=segment_name();
        #revenue=sales_Rev_turn(fpt=q, fpr=range(2023Q3, 2024Q3));
        )
    get(#segment, #revenue)
    for(segments('GTN US Equity',type=reported,hierarchy=PRODUCT, level=1))
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    results = bq.bql(query)
    df = results.combine().pivot(
        index="PERIOD_END_DATE", on="#segment", values="#revenue"
    )
    print(df)

docs.title: BSRCH
docs.text:
Use case: Excel-style searches (SRCH/BI domains). Good for running saved SRCH screens or Bloomberg BI templates.

A failed search raises BloombergError (a ValueError), and a search without results gives an empty frame that keeps its columns.

Key points: - Column types follow what Bloomberg sends (StringValue or DoubleValue): a number sent as text stays a string, and a blank cell in a numeric column becomes null. - Pass overrides as a dict or as (name, value) pairs; values are stringified. Common keys: LIMIT to raise the row cap (default ~5k), custom keys like BIKEY for BI templates, or domain-specific parameters.

docs.title: Example: two COCO bonds (LIMIT=2)
docs.text:
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bsrch("FI:SRCHEX.@COCO", overrides={"LIMIT": 2})
    print(df)
